title: THE ARBITER AT THE CROSSROADS OF UNIVERSES
deck: Forty thousand people have nine days, and the only door charges each of them what they would most grieve to lose. Illuminara can cross for nothing, which makes her useless as a witness, so she asks the gatekeeper what no one has asked it: what it is trying to find out.
shape: Six scenes over three days at the Sill: a camp ready to storm the door, a gatekeeper that explains its toll, a child's question that moves the measure from before the crossing to after it and a bond that answers the gatekeeper's own objection, a valley hall that counts its roofs and refuses in part, ten families who cross on that bond, and a ledger and a door that can finally carry everyone.

scenes.title: Nine Days
paragraphs: *The Sill, near-side camp · dusk, nine days before Orrel's sky comes apart*

Eleven days ago the line to the Sill had been two kilometres long. Now it was a gap in the tents, and Corvin Hale stood in the gap with three thousand people behind him, holding pry bars, tent poles and the long mooring hooks of the Orrel docks.

Beyond the camp the ground stopped being ground. A bridge of standing light crossed a dark with no far wall, and at its end a lit doorway showed a green valley where sixty-one families sat on benches and looked at nothing.
Illuminara had walked the bridge and back before anyone thought to stop her. Nothing had asked her for anything. That, more than the bars and hooks, was what frightened the camp.

**Hale**  
You went over and came back whole. Good. Then you will see why we take the door at first light. Sixty-one families paid its price, and you can watch what they have become from here.
A child of nine stood at his elbow, not holding his hand, with her chin up and her eyes on the doorway.

**Tam**  
My mother is the one in the blue coat. She waves at everybody. The door lets us hear a little, and she asked the ferryman whose little girl I was.

**Hale**  
It lets one family through every quarter hour, and every family pays. That is ninety-six families a day. Nine days make eight hundred and sixty-four. We are nine thousand families. I will say that once more and then we go in with what we have.

**Illuminara**  
I could close that bridge until dawn, and you would never forgive me, and it would not change one of those numbers. So I won't. I would like to know what it is asking before you break it. What do you think it wants?

**Hale**  
What we love. It takes it. That is a tax, not a question.

**Illuminara**  
A tax takes the same from everyone. This takes the thing each person would miss most. Whatever does that is trying to find something out. Give me until the middle of the night to learn what.
He looked down at the child, and at the bridge, and at the nine thousand families he could not count fast enough.

**Hale**  
Until first light. Not a breath after.

scenes.title: The Coin
paragraphs: *The head of the bridge · midnight*

What waited at the other end of the light was not a creature. It was the sense of being considered, very exactly, by something that had considered a great many people and found most of them smaller than their words.

**The Arbiter**  
You paid nothing. I looked at what you would grieve, and it is there, and my rule could not take it. The toll binds a traveller who asks for ground. You asked for nothing, so it had no hold on you. Go back, and do not call that a passage.

**Illuminara**  
I am not asking to cross. I came to ask what you are looking for. Not what you take. What you are looking for.
The light did not move for a long time.

**The Arbiter**  
In all my years, no one has asked that.

It told her without self-pity, the way an old surveyor names the river that took a bridge. Four hundred winters ago eleven thousand of the Kest had come to the door with their dead on carts and asked only for ground to bury them in. Every word they said was true when they said it, and the door had opened for the words. By spring the valley beyond it, the Dun Reach, was burning, and the people burning it were the people who had wept at the door.

**The Arbiter**  
I could not read what they would do. I could read what they would give. So now I take from each traveller the one thing they would most grieve to lose. A conqueror will say anything. He will not hand over what he loves best for a land he means to burn. Every other way of knowing a traveller has been lied to. Grief cannot be counterfeited. Offer me another coin.

**Illuminara**  
I have lived among these people for a day. They are afraid, not dangerous. I will vouch for them.

**The Arbiter**  
I do not know you. Your word is not a coin.

**Illuminara**  
No. And you must not count me. Your door could not reach me because I asked it for nothing. That is a fact about your door. It is not evidence about forty thousand people who will ask it for everything, and I will not have it cited for them, now or later.
It was the first thing she had said that the light seemed to weigh.

She sat down at the head of the bridge, because standing made this a bargain between powers and she did not want to be a power here. *If I am wrong, tomorrow ten thousand people are on that bridge on my word.*

**Illuminara**  
I have things I would grieve to lose. It is your rule that cannot reach them, not their absence. So I can only put something on the table by choice. Look at this. I am afraid. Not of you. I am afraid of being the reason they walk onto that bridge, and of being wrong about the reason.

**The Arbiter**  
That is honest. It is not a coin. It is the first thing anyone has shown me at this door that I could not have taken.

scenes.title: After
paragraphs: *The head of the bridge · a little after midnight*
Small feet make no sound on a bridge of light, so Illuminara did not hear Tam until she stood beside her.

**Illuminara**  
Tam. You cannot be here. It will ask you for the price.

**Tam**  
I know. I'm not crossing. I came to ask it something, and nobody has asked it the right thing yet because they are all too frightened.
The Arbiter turned toward the child with a patience Illuminara had not known it had.

**The Arbiter**  
Ask.

**Tam**  
What happens to us after you stop looking?

**The Arbiter**  
I do not stop looking at the door.

**Tam**  
Not the door. Us. When we're over. Do you look at my mama?
The light was slow to answer.

**The Arbiter**  
I hold the door. I see what the door sees. I do not see the valley.

**Illuminara**  
In four hundred winters, how long have you watched any traveller after you let them through?

**The Arbiter**  
Not for the length of a breath.

Illuminara felt the shape of it seat, the way a joint does when the last pin goes in. The toll was a measurement taken at the one moment it could be taken and never checked against what came after. It could say what a person would grieve. It had never learned what a person would do.

**Illuminara**  
No one who paid has burned the valley while you were looking. You were never looking. So tell me what you would have to see. Not what you could take. What you would have to see.

**The Arbiter**  
Their hands in a stranger's house. Whether the house still stands in a season. Someone on that side who knows the place and would lose something real if they were wrong. And a way to undo it if they are.

**Illuminara**  
That is a host. A hearth that stands behind its guests.

**The Arbiter**  
A host's welcome is not proof. A host can be deceived as I was deceived. And the only undoing I have is to close the door behind a cohort, which shuts out those who kept faith and strands the one who did not among the people he would hurt.

**Illuminara**  
Then the bond must fall on the person who breaks it and on no one else. A guest pledges to the household that lodges them: no arms raised, nothing taken that is not given, and an answer to the valley's own moot for any harm.

**The Arbiter**  
And the host? You have given the host nothing to lose, and I need someone who would.

**Illuminara**  
The roof-right. The standing to say who sleeps under it. A guest's hands never cost a host that. Hiding a breach does, and then the roof is struck from the ledger. The host loses a place to shelter people, not the house.

**The Arbiter**  
And the guest who breaks it, in a house I cannot enter?

**Illuminara**  
You do not enter. You recall one person, the one who broke the bond, and not their family. Not to the camp, which will not stand past the ninth day. On the valley side of your door there is a warden's house of stone, in your sight, with a hearth and a well and a roof that will outlast Orrel's sky. You bring the guest there and no further. The moot sits within three days, and the guest goes home to their household when the moot and the person harmed say it is mended. No one goes back through the door to a failing world. You are the moot's witness, not its judge. And if hosts ever hide a breach, you may stand the door at the threshold to new cohorts until the moot says why.

**The Arbiter**  
Forty-eight hours in ten houses proves nothing about a season.

**Illuminara**  
It proves you can see and you can recall. The season is the test, and the recall holds for all seventy days. The forty-eight hours test the door, not the people. Ten families first, each cohort larger only while no bond is hidden. And anyone who would rather pay the old toll may.

**The Arbiter**  
And if the hosts will not stand?

**Illuminara**  
Then nothing opens, and I will tell Hale so at first light. I cannot promise you a host. Only they can.

**Tam**  
Can I ask one more?

**The Arbiter**  
Ask.

**Tam**  
If my mama wanted back what you took, would you give it?

**The Arbiter**  
No one has asked. I have kept every one. A toll is paid once, but I have never thrown one away.

scenes.title: The Ford Custom
paragraphs: *Dun Reach, the reeve's hall · two in the morning*

A black beam ran the length of the hall's ceiling, charred through at the middle and propped with a newer timber. Odile Brannock, the reeve, sat under it with a ledger and a pot of tea she did not offer to share until she had heard everything.

**Brannock**  
That is from the last time strangers asked this valley for a roof. Look at it. The black is real.

**Illuminara**  
I know. I am not asking you to forget it. I am asking you to put your own roof behind a stranger and let something watch to see whether you were right.

**Brannock**  
We took the sixty-one without a vote, because when the river rises you open the loft and ask nothing. That is the ford custom. You want it for forty thousand. Twenty-one thousand hearths in six towns, eleven thousand with a loft or a barn fit for a family, nine thousand families coming. Seven hundred go to the threshold houses, the wardens' inns and the door-yard lodges. I have walked every one this week. Each has a hearth and a well, and each stands within sight of the door. That leaves eight thousand three hundred, and if each roof takes one I need three of every four with room to say yes. They will not.

**Illuminara**  
Then each roof may take two if it wants to. That is four thousand one hundred and fifty roofs, a little over one in three of those with room.

**Brannock**  
And when a guest breaks it? My people burned once for strangers' hands, and they will ask whose roof pays.

**Illuminara**  
No roof pays for a guest's hands. The guest answers to your moot, and until it sits the Arbiter may bring that one guest, and no one else, to the warden's house at the door. A roof-right is lost only if its host hides a breach.
Brannock wrote a line in the margin before she answered.

**Brannock**  
The moot is mine to call: the reeve, two hosts by lot and one guest the guests choose. It has judged goats and boundary stones for two hundred years. It can judge hands. That I can sign. So can the warden's house. It has stood empty since the burning, and it has a roof.
Tobiah Greer, who kept the valley's granaries, had not sat down. There was flour in the creases of his sleeves.

**Greer**  
You are asking me to say yes to the thing that burned us. I will say it plainly. The last strangers cried at our door too.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. They were believed, and you were right to learn from it. That is why this is not a promise. It is a roof you can see, a recall that falls on one person, and a season to watch.

**Greer**  
Grain, then. My granaries hold bread for forty thousand more mouths for seventy days, if we all eat less. After that, what? I will not stake my children's winter on a stranger's good faith.

**Illuminara**  
Then the bond runs seventy days, and at the end the guests plant, or go back to the threshold houses, or stay by their hosts' choice, and everyone looks again. You do not have to host. Will you count?

**Greer**  
Count what?

**Illuminara**  
The grain. Honestly, and aloud, with the number chalked on the door. Nobody here should say yes to a figure they cannot check.
He stood a while with his cap in his hands. Then he put it on the table.

**Greer**  
I will count it. I will not house anyone. Do not let my neighbours be ashamed of me for that.

**Brannock**  
Nobody will be.

She turned the ledger, wrote the first line, and signed her roof-right under it: *Brannock, the reeve's hall, two families.* By four o'clock nine more had signed and runners had gone out to the six towns with the pages. On the back leaf she had begun a second column, for those who would sign only after they had watched.

scenes.title: Ten Families
paragraphs: *The Sill, first light · the next morning*
Hale heard the terms standing, with the camp pressed close behind him.

**Hale**  
Ten families. Forty-eight hours. We have nine days.

**Illuminara**  
It is forty-three people, and it is the cheapest test we have. If it fails, you have lost two days and not your sky, and you can still do what you came to do. If it works, the door widens.

**Hale**  
Nobody is assigned a roof. A family that dislikes its host waits for another. A family that wants the old toll pays it. And nine of the ten places go by lot, not by who I like.
The tenth the camp voted itself, with no one speaking against it. It went to Tam and her aunt, because Tam's mother was on the far side in a blue coat.

The three thousand set their pry bars in a cart. Some of them, without being told, picked up the luggage of the families who were going. Each of the ten said its pledge aloud at the head of the bridge, to the host it had drawn: no arms raised, nothing taken that was not given, an answer to the moot.
Tam stopped at the head of the bridge. Illuminara did not carry her.

**Illuminara**  
You can stay. You can cross. Either is yours to say.

**Tam**  
I'm crossing. I would like to be asked first, though.
The light asked her, in its way, and what it asked was only whether she meant to come as a guest. She said yes. Nothing was taken.

Ten hosts waited at the far end with their roof-rights signed, and the Arbiter's attention lay on them as lightly as a hand on a table. Among the hollowed families a woman in a blue coat was waving at everyone.

**Tam**  
I'm Tam. You taught me to whistle through a blade of grass. You don't have to know me.

**Ansa**  
I'm sorry. I don't. I wish I did. You look as if you have walked a long way.
Illuminara went to the doorway of the guest-house, where the Arbiter could be spoken to, and spoke to it quietly.

**Illuminara**  
She is here, and she may want to ask. Will you answer her?

**The Arbiter**  
Let her.

**Ansa**  
Ask what? I don't know what I lost.

**The Arbiter**  
A daughter, and eleven days of not knowing her. If you take it back you take both.

**Ansa**  
Then I will take both.
There was no light. Ansa simply stopped, and put her hand flat to her mouth, and said Tam's name in the voice that is used only for that name.
Before noon eleven more of the sixty had asked the same question. Four of them said no, because they had begun again here and wished to go on from it, and they were not argued with.

scenes.title: A Street Wide
paragraphs: *The Sill, dawn · the third day*
For forty-eight hours the Arbiter had looked through the door into ten houses, and it spoke at the head of the bridge with the camp pressed close to hear.

**The Arbiter**  
Nothing has burned. On the first evening a guest shoved his host's son over a goat. The host said so before dark, as pledged. I brought that one man to the warden's house, and no one of his household. The moot sat in the barn at noon the next day, the guest mended the fence, and by dusk he was home with his wife and sons. I closed nothing. In four hundred winters I had never watched a bond tested. I will open the door a street wide, only as far as the ledger holds the roofs. I will recall one person at the moot's word, and no more than that. I will take no toll, and I will not refuse a family that chooses to pay one.

**Hale**  
How many today?

**The Arbiter**  
Six hundred and fifty.

A runner came across the bridge with the reeve's ledger, carried up through the night. The second column had emptied. The ones who had written *watch first* had watched the same forty-eight hours from their loft windows, and four thousand three hundred and ten roofs were signed against four thousand one hundred and fifty needed, a hundred and sixty to spare.

Hale pinned the schedule to the post in his square hand: forty-three on the first day, six hundred and fifty on this one, then twenty-four hundred, five thousand, eight thousand, nine thousand five hundred, nine thousand, and fifty-four hundred and seven on the ninth. Forty thousand people, nine thousand families, seven hundred families in the threshold houses and eight thousand three hundred under the signed roofs. If a hundred and sixty roofs withdrew, the reserve would hold exactly. If more did, the Arbiter would open only as far as the roofs held, and the old toll stayed open to anyone who chose it.

**Hale**  
Can the door carry that? Housing was never the whole of it.

**The Arbiter**  
Opened a street wide, it passes ten thousand between dawn and dusk. Your largest day is nine thousand five hundred. I kept the door narrow for four hundred winters, but I did not forget its width. Each day's number opens only if the day before it hid no bond. If one is hidden, that day waits until the moot has said why. The last three days have room for six thousand more than you have posted, so a short hold can be absorbed. A long one cannot, and everyone on this bridge knows it. The threshold houses lie in my sight. I counted them last night: beds for seven hundred families, none more, and I count them with the roofs.
Everyone on the bridge knew where the schedule could fail, and where it could not.
Some families took the old toll anyway. A widower from the docks went first. They had reasons, and the door held for them too.

Hale had put his bars in the cart and taken a slate and a stub of chalk. He would cross last, and had said so, and no one had asked him to. He stood at the head of the line counting people through, aloud, one number to each.

On the far side Tam sat on a gatepost beside a woman in a blue coat, whistling through a blade of grass, badly. Illuminara stood at the edge of the light, which was a hand's breadth wider than yesterday, and listened to the counting go on behind her in the dark.

critic_line: Illuminara first learns that the Arbiter's cruel toll is an evidence system built after a true welcome ended in fire, then helps it replace untested grief with a voluntary host bond, a valley moot, individual recall to a surviving safe house and observable conduct; Tam, Brannock, Greer, Hale, the hosts and the guests retain consequential choice, forty-three people cross intact, the first breach is repaired without collective punishment, the door and signed roofs can carry all forty thousand within nine days, and earlier travellers may freely reclaim both love and pain without erasing the valley's history or the remaining risk of a long hidden breach.

shared_strengths: Strong premise and humane resolution: asking the gatekeeper what it seeks, Tam's questions, the blue-coat reunion. Dialogue-heavy as these readers like. Mid-story logistics (roof counts, schedules, bond mechanics) read like a spreadsheet and sap momentum, and the solution comes somewhat smoothly.

A compelling moral puzzle becomes humane institutional design through intelligent dialogue, concrete stakes, and a deeply earned reunion. The procedural arithmetic and repeated bond mechanics may feel over-explained, but the premise, compassionate choices, and satisfying transformation of the gatekeeper should carry most target readers through and remain memorable.

translation_sl.title: RAZSODNIK NA KRIŽIŠČU VESOLJ
translation_sl.deck: Štirideset tisoč ljudi ima devet dni, edina vrata pa vsakemu zaračunajo tisto, kar bi najbolj objokoval, če bi izgubil. Illuminara lahko prečka brez plačila, zaradi česar je kot priča neuporabna, zato vratarja vpraša nekaj, česar ga ni vprašal še nihče: kaj skuša ugotoviti.
translation_sl.shape: Šest prizorov v treh dneh pri Pragu: tabor, pripravljen, da zavzame vrata, vratar, ki pojasni svojo cestnino, otrokovo vprašanje, ki merilo premakne s časa pred prehodom na čas po njem, in zaveza, ki odgovori na vratarjev lastni ugovor, dolinska dvorana, ki prešteje svoje strehe in deloma odkloni, deset družin, ki prečkajo po tej zavezi, ter knjiga in vrata, ki lahko končno prenesejo vse.

scenes.title: Devet dni
paragraphs: *Tabor na bližnji strani Praga · mrak, devet dni preden se razkolje Orrelovo nebo*

Pred enajstimi dnevi je bila vrsta do Praga dolga dva kilometra. Zdaj je bila v šotorih vrzel, v njej pa je stal Corvin Hale s tri tisoč ljudmi za seboj, ki so držali lomilke, šotorske palice in dolge privezne kavlje z Orrelovih dokov.

Za taborom so tla prenehala biti tla. Most iz pokončne svetlobe je prečkal temo brez oddaljene stene, na njegovem koncu pa so osvetljena vrata kazala zeleno dolino, kjer je enainšestdeset družin sedelo na klopeh in strmelo v nič.
Illuminara je šla čez most in nazaj, preden je komur koli prišlo na misel, da bi jo ustavil. Nič je ni prosilo za nič. Prav to je tabor prestrašilo bolj kot palice in kavlji.

**Hale**  
Šla si čez in se vrnila cela. Dobro. Potem razumeš, zakaj bomo vrata zavzeli ob prvi svetlobi. Enainšestdeset družin je plačalo njihovo ceno in od tod lahko vidiš, kaj je ostalo od njih.
Ob njegovem komolcu je stal devetletni otrok, ki ga ni držal za roko, z dvignjeno brado in očmi, uprtimi v vrata.

**Tam**  
Moja mama je tista v modrem plašču. Vsem maha. Vrata nam pustijo malo slišati in vprašala me je, čigava deklica sem.

**Hale**  
Spustijo eno družino skozi vsake četrt ure in vsaka družina plača. To je šestindevetdeset družin na dan. Devet dni pomeni osemsto štiriinšestdeset. Nas je devet tisoč družin. To bom povedal še enkrat, potem pa gremo noter s tem, kar imamo.

**Illuminara**  
Ta most bi lahko zaprla do zore, pa mi ne bi nikoli odpustili in nobena od teh številk se ne bi spremenila. Zato ga ne bom. Preden ga razbijete, bi rada izvedela, kaj sprašuje. Kaj misliš, da hoče?

**Hale**  
Kar ljubimo. To nam vzame. To je davek, ne vprašanje.

**Illuminara**  
Davek vsem vzame isto. To pa vsakemu vzame stvar, ki bi jo najbolj pogrešal. Karkoli to počne, skuša nekaj ugotoviti. Daj mi čas do polnoči, da izvem kaj.
Pogledal je otroka, most in devet tisoč družin, ki jih ni mogel dovolj hitro prešteti.

**Hale**  
Do prve svetlobe. Niti za en dih dlje.

scenes.title: Kovanec
paragraphs: *Začetek mostu · polnoč*
Na drugem koncu svetlobe ni čakalo bitje. Bil je občutek, da jo nekaj zelo natančno presoja — nekaj, kar je presodilo že zelo veliko ljudi in ugotovilo, da je večina manjša od svojih besed.

**Razsodnik**  
Ničesar nisi plačala. Pogledal sem, za čim bi žalovala, in to je tam, moje pravilo pa tega ni moglo vzeti. Cestnina zaveže popotnika, ki prosi za tla. Ti nisi prosila za nič, zato nad teboj ni imela moči. Vrni se in temu ne reci prehod.

**Illuminara**  
Ne prosim za prehod. Prišla sem vprašat, kaj iščeš. Ne, kaj vzameš. Kaj iščeš.
Svetloba se dolgo ni premaknila.

**Razsodnik**  
V vseh mojih letih tega ni vprašal nihče.

Povedal ji je brez samopomilovanja, kakor star zemljemerec poimenuje reko, ki je odnesla most. Pred štiristo zimami je enajst tisoč Kestov prišlo k vratom z mrtvimi na vozovih in prosilo samo za tla, v katera bi jih pokopali. Vsaka njihova beseda je bila resnična v trenutku, ko so jo izrekli, in vrata so se zaradi teh besed odprla. Do pomladi je gorela dolina onkraj njih, Dun Reach, zažigali pa so jo ljudje, ki so jokali pred vrati.

**Razsodnik**  
Nisem mogel prebrati, kaj bodo storili. Lahko sem prebral, kaj bodo dali. Zato zdaj vsakemu popotniku vzamem tisto, kar bi najbolj objokoval, če bi izgubil. Osvajalec bo rekel karkoli. Ne bo izročil tega, kar najbolj ljubi, za deželo, ki jo namerava požgati. Vsak drug način spoznavanja popotnika je bil preslepljen. Žalosti ni mogoče ponarediti. Ponudi mi drug kovanec.

**Illuminara**  
Med temi ljudmi živim en dan. Prestrašeni so, ne nevarni. Jamčila bom zanje.

**Razsodnik**  
Ne poznam te. Tvoja beseda ni kovanec.

**Illuminara**  
Ni. In mene ne smeš šteti. Tvoja vrata me niso mogla doseči, ker jih nisem prosila za nič. To je dejstvo o tvojih vratih. Ni dokaz o štirideset tisoč ljudeh, ki jih bodo prosili za vse, in ne bom dovolila, da bi ga navajali zanje, zdaj ali pozneje.
To je bilo prvo, kar je rekla, pa se je zdelo, da svetloba to tehta.
Sedla je ob začetku mostu, ker bi stoje to spremenila v kupčijo med silami, ona pa tu ni hotela biti sila. *Če se motim, bo jutri deset tisoč ljudi stopilo na ta most na mojo besedo.*

**Illuminara**  
Imam stvari, katerih izgubo bi objokovala. Tvoje pravilo jih ne more doseči, ne pa da jih ni. Zato lahko nekaj položim na mizo samo po lastni izbiri. Poglej to. Strah me je. Ne tebe. Strah me je, da bom razlog, da stopijo na ta most, in da se motim o razlogu.

**Razsodnik**  
To je iskreno. Ni kovanec. Je pa prva stvar, ki mi jo je kdo pokazal pred temi vrati, pa je ne bi mogel vzeti.

scenes.title: Potem
paragraphs: *Začetek mostu · malo po polnoči*
Majhne noge na mostu iz svetlobe ne povzročajo zvoka, zato Illuminara ni slišala Tam, dokler ni stala ob njej.

**Illuminara**  
Tam. Ne smeš biti tukaj. Vprašalo te bo po ceni.

**Tam**  
Vem. Ne bom prečkala. Prišla sem ga nekaj vprašat in nihče ga še ni vprašal prave stvari, ker jih je vse preveč strah.
Razsodnik se je obrnil k otroku s potrpežljivostjo, za katero Illuminara ni vedela, da jo premore.

**Razsodnik**  
Vprašaj.

**Tam**  
Kaj se zgodi z nami, ko nehaš gledati?

**Razsodnik**  
Vrat ne neham gledati.

**Tam**  
Ne vrat. Nas. Ko smo čez. Ali gledaš mojo mamo?
Svetloba je odgovorila počasi.

**Razsodnik**  
Držim vrata. Vidim, kar vidijo vrata. Doline ne vidim.

**Illuminara**  
Kako dolgo si v štiristo zimah opazoval katerega koli popotnika potem, ko si ga spustil skozi?

**Razsodnik**  
Niti za en dih.

Illuminara je začutila, kako se je oblika usedla, kot se usede sklep, ko je vstavljen zadnji zatič. Cestnina je bila meritev, opravljena v edinem trenutku, ko jo je bilo mogoče opraviti, in nikoli preverjena glede na to, kar je sledilo. Lahko je povedala, za čim bi človek žaloval. Nikoli pa se ni naučila, kaj bi človek storil.

**Illuminara**  
Nihče, ki je plačal, ni požgal doline, medtem ko si gledal. Nikoli nisi gledal. Zato mi povej, kaj bi moral videti. Ne, kaj bi lahko vzel. Kaj bi moral videti.

**Razsodnik**  
Njihove roke v tuji hiši. Ali hiša po enem letnem času še stoji. Nekoga na oni strani, ki pozna kraj in bi izgubil nekaj resničnega, če bi se motil. In način, da se stvar razveljavi, če se moti.

**Illuminara**  
To je gostitelj. Ognjišče, ki jamči za svoje goste.

**Razsodnik**  
Gostiteljeva dobrodošlica ni dokaz. Gostitelj je lahko preslepljen, kakor sem bil jaz. In edina razveljavitev, ki jo imam, je zapreti vrata za skupino, s čimer izključim tiste, ki so držali besedo, in tistega, ki je ni, pustim med ljudmi, ki bi jim škodil.

**Illuminara**  
Potem mora zaveza pasti na človeka, ki jo prekrši, in na nikogar drugega. Gost se zaveže gospodinjstvu, ki ga nastani: ne bo dvignil orožja, ne bo vzel ničesar, kar mu ni dano, in za vsako škodo bo odgovarjal pred dolinskim zborom.

**Razsodnik**  
In gostitelj? Gostitelju nisi dala ničesar, kar bi lahko izgubil, jaz pa potrebujem nekoga, ki bi lahko.

**Illuminara**  
Pravico do strehe. Pravico odločati, kdo spi pod njo. Gostova dejanja gostitelja nikoli ne stanejo te pravice. Prikrivanje kršitve pa ga, in tedaj se streha izbriše iz knjige. Gostitelj izgubi prostor za zavetje ljudi, ne hiše.

**Razsodnik**  
In gost, ki jo prekrši v hiši, v katero ne morem vstopiti?

**Illuminara**  
Ne vstopiš. Odpokličeš eno osebo, tisto, ki je prekršila zavezo, ne njene družine. Ne v tabor, ki ne bo stal po devetem dnevu. Na dolinski strani tvojih vrat je kamnita oskrbnikova hiša, ki jo vidiš, z ognjiščem, vodnjakom in streho, ki bo preživela Orrelovo nebo. Gosta pripelješ tja in nikamor dlje. Zbor zasede v treh dneh, gost pa se vrne domov k svojemu gospodinjstvu, ko zbor in oškodovani povesta, da je škoda popravljena. Nihče se ne vrne skozi vrata v propadajoči svet. Ti si priča zbora, ne njegov sodnik. In če bi gostitelji kdaj prikrili kršitev, smeš vrata ustaviti na pragu novih skupin, dokler zbor ne pove zakaj.

**Razsodnik**  
Oseminštirideset ur v desetih hišah ne dokazuje ničesar o letnem času.

**Illuminara**  
Dokazuje, da lahko vidiš in odpokličeš. Letni čas je preizkus, odpoklic pa velja vseh sedemdeset dni. Oseminštirideset ur preizkusi vrata, ne ljudi. Najprej deset družin, vsaka skupina pa je večja samo, dokler ni prikrita nobena zaveza. In kdor bi raje plačal staro cestnino, jo lahko.

**Razsodnik**  
In če gostitelji ne bodo jamčili?

**Illuminara**  
Potem se nič ne odpre in ob prvi svetlobi bom to povedala Halu. Gostitelja ti ne morem obljubiti. To lahko storijo samo oni.

**Tam**  
Lahko vprašam še nekaj?

**Razsodnik**  
Vprašaj.

**Tam**  
Če bi moja mama hotela nazaj, kar si ji vzel, bi ji to dal?

**Razsodnik**  
Nihče ni vprašal. Vse sem obdržal. Cestnina se plača enkrat, vendar nisem ničesar zavrgel.

scenes.title: Običaj pri brodu
paragraphs: *Dun Reach, županjina dvorana · dve zjutraj*

Črn tram je potekal po vsej dolžini stropa dvorane, na sredini prežgan in podprt z novejšim lesom. Odile Brannock, županja, je sedela pod njim s knjigo in čajnikom, iz katerega ni ponudila čaja, dokler ni slišala vsega.

**Brannock**  
To je od zadnjič, ko so tujci prosili to dolino za streho. Poglej. Črnina je resnična.

**Illuminara**  
Vem. Ne prosim te, da jo pozabiš. Prosim te, da za tujca jamčiš z lastno streho in pustiš nečemu opazovati, ali si imela prav.

**Brannock**  
Enainšestdeset smo sprejeli brez glasovanja, ker ob narasli reki odpreš podstrešje in ničesar ne vprašaš. To je običaj pri brodu. Ti hočeš isto za štirideset tisoč. V šestih mestih je enaindvajset tisoč ognjišč, enajst tisoč jih ima podstrešje ali skedenj, primeren za družino, prihaja pa devet tisoč družin. Sedemsto jih gre v hiše ob pragu, oskrbniške gostilne in prenočišča ob vratih. Ta teden sem prehodila vsako. Vsaka ima ognjišče in vodnjak in vsaka stoji v vidnem polju vrat. Ostane osem tisoč tristo, in če vsaka streha sprejme eno, morajo privoliti tri od štirih, ki imajo prostor. Ne bodo.

**Illuminara**  
Potem lahko vsaka streha sprejme dve družini, če želi. To je štiri tisoč sto petdeset streh, malo več kot ena od treh, ki imajo prostor.

**Brannock**  
In ko gost prekrši zavezo? Moji ljudje so enkrat že goreli zaradi rok tujcev in vprašali bodo, čigava streha plača.

**Illuminara**  
Nobena streha ne plača za gostova dejanja. Gost odgovarja pred vašim zborom, dokler ta ne zasede, pa sme Razsodnik tistega enega gosta, in nikogar drugega, pripeljati v oskrbnikovo hišo pri vratih. Pravica do strehe se izgubi samo, če gostitelj prikrije kršitev.
Brannock je v rob zapisala vrstico, preden je odgovorila.

**Brannock**  
Zbor skličem jaz: županja, dva z žrebom izbrana gostitelja in en gost, ki ga izberejo gostje. Dvesto let je sodil o kozah in mejnih kamnih. Lahko sodi o dejanjih. To lahko podpišem. Tudi oskrbnikova hiša lahko. Od požiga je prazna in ima streho.
Tobiah Greer, ki je skrbel za dolinske kašče, ni sedel. V gubah njegovih rokavov je bila moka.

**Greer**  
Prosiš me, naj privolim v stvar, ki nas je požgala. Povedal bom naravnost. Tudi zadnji tujci so jokali pred našimi vrati.

**Illuminara**  
Da. Verjeli ste jim in prav je, da ste se iz tega kaj naučili. Zato to ni obljuba. To je streha, ki jo lahko vidiš, odpoklic, ki pade na eno osebo, in letni čas za opazovanje.

**Greer**  
Žito torej. Moje kašče imajo kruha za štirideset tisoč dodatnih ust za sedemdeset dni, če bomo vsi jedli manj. Kaj pa potem? Zime svojih otrok ne bom zastavil za dobro vero tujca.

**Illuminara**  
Potem zaveza velja sedemdeset dni, na koncu pa gostje posejejo, se vrnejo v hiše ob pragu ali ostanejo po izbiri gostiteljev, nato pa vsi znova presodijo. Ni ti treba gostiti. Boš štel?

**Greer**  
Štel kaj?

**Illuminara**  
Žito. Pošteno in naglas, številka pa naj bo s kredo zapisana na vratih. Nihče tu ne bi smel privoliti v številko, ki je ne more preveriti.
Nekaj časa je stal s čepico v rokah. Nato jo je položil na mizo.

**Greer**  
Preštel ga bom. Nikogar ne bom nastanil. Ne dovolite, da bi se me sosedje zaradi tega sramovali.

**Brannock**  
Nihče se te ne bo.

Obrnila je knjigo, zapisala prvo vrstico in pod njo podpisala svojo pravico do strehe: *Brannock, županjina dvorana, dve družini.* Do štirih zjutraj jih je podpisalo še devet, sli pa so s stranmi odšli v šest mest. Na zadnjem listu je začela drugi stolpec za tiste, ki bi podpisali šele po tem, ko bi opazovali.

scenes.title: Deset družin
paragraphs: *Prag, prva svetloba · naslednje jutro*
Hale je pogoje poslušal stoje, tabor pa se je tesno stiskal za njim.

**Hale**  
Deset družin. Oseminštirideset ur. Imamo devet dni.

**Illuminara**  
Triinštirideset ljudi je in to je najcenejši preizkus, kar jih imamo. Če spodleti, izgubiš dva dneva, ne svojega neba, in še vedno lahko storiš, kar si prišel storit. Če uspe, se vrata razširijo.

**Hale**  
Nikomur ne bo dodeljena streha. Družina, ki ji gostitelj ni všeč, počaka na drugega. Družina, ki želi staro cestnino, jo plača. Devet od desetih mest pa bo izbranih z žrebom, ne po tem, kdo je meni všeč.
Deseto je tabor izglasoval sam, ne da bi kdo nasprotoval. Pripadlo je Tam in njeni teti, ker je bila Tamina mati na drugi strani v modrem plašču.

Tri tisoč ljudi je lomilke zložilo na voz. Nekateri so, ne da bi jim kdo naročil, pobrali prtljago družin, ki so odhajale. Vsaka od desetih je ob začetku mostu svojemu izžrebanemu gostitelju naglas izrekla svojo zavezo: nobenega dvignjenega orožja, ničesar, kar jim ni dano, in odgovor pred zborom.
Tam se je ustavila ob začetku mostu. Illuminara je ni nesla.

**Illuminara**  
Lahko ostaneš. Lahko prečkaš. Oboje je tvoja odločitev.

**Tam**  
Prečkala bom. Rada pa bi, da me najprej vprašajo.
Svetloba jo je na svoj način vprašala in vprašanje je bilo samo, ali namerava priti kot gostja. Rekla je da. Nič ji ni bilo vzeto.

Na drugem koncu je čakalo deset gostiteljev s podpisanimi pravicami do strehe, Razsodnikova pozornost pa je ležala na njih lahno kot dlan na mizi. Med izpraznjenimi družinami je vsem mahala ženska v modrem plašču.

**Tam**  
Jaz sem Tam. Naučila si me žvižgati skozi travno bilko. Ni ti treba vedeti, kdo sem.

**Ansa**  
Žal mi je. Ne vem. Videti si, kot da si prehodila dolgo pot.
Illuminara je šla k vratom hiše za goste, kjer se je bilo mogoče pogovarjati z Razsodnikom, in ga tiho nagovorila.

**Illuminara**  
Tukaj je in morda bo hotela vprašati. Ji boš odgovoril?

**Razsodnik**  
Naj vpraša.

**Ansa**  
Kaj naj vprašam? Ne vem, kaj sem izgubila.

**Razsodnik**  
Hčer in enajst dni, ko je nisi poznala. Če to vzameš nazaj, vzameš oboje.

**Ansa**  
Potem bom vzela oboje.
Ni bilo svetlobe. Ansa se je preprosto ustavila, si z dlanjo pokrila usta in izgovorila Tamino ime z glasom, ki se uporablja samo za to ime.
Pred poldnevom je enako vprašalo še enajst od šestdesetih. Štirje so rekli ne, ker so tu začeli znova in so želeli nadaljevati od tam, in nihče se ni prepiral z njimi.

scenes.title: Široko kot ulica
paragraphs: *Prag, zora · tretji dan*
Razsodnik je oseminštirideset ur skozi vrata gledal v deset hiš, nato pa je spregovoril ob začetku mostu, medtem ko se je tabor tesno stiskal, da bi slišal.

**Razsodnik**  
Nič ni zgorelo. Prvi večer je gost zaradi koze porinil gostiteljevega sina. Gostitelj je to, kot se je zavezal, povedal še pred mrakom. Tistega enega moškega sem pripeljal v oskrbnikovo hišo, nikogar iz njegovega gospodinjstva. Zbor je naslednji dan opoldne zasedel v skednju, gost je popravil ograjo in do mraka je bil doma pri ženi in sinovih. Ničesar nisem zaprl. V štiristo zimah še nikoli nisem opazoval preizkušene zaveze. Vrata bom odprl tako široko kot ulico, vendar le toliko, kolikor knjiga vsebuje streh. Odpoklical bom eno osebo po besedi zbora in nikoli več kot to. Ne bom vzel cestnine in ne bom zavrnil družine, ki se odloči, da jo plača.

**Hale**  
Koliko danes?

**Razsodnik**  
Šeststo petdeset.

Čez most je pritekel sel z županjino knjigo, ki so jo ponoči prinesli od hiše do hiše. Drugi stolpec se je izpraznil. Tisti, ki so zapisali *najprej bom opazoval*, so istih oseminštirideset ur opazovali iz svojih podstrešnih oken, podpisanih pa je bilo štiri tisoč tristo deset streh, čeprav jih je bilo potrebnih štiri tisoč sto petdeset — sto šestdeset več.

Hale je z razločnimi velikimi črkami pripel urnik na steber: triinštirideset prvi dan, šeststo petdeset ta dan, nato dva tisoč štiristo, pet tisoč, osem tisoč, devet tisoč petsto, devet tisoč in pet tisoč štiristo sedem deveti dan. Štirideset tisoč ljudi, devet tisoč družin, sedemsto družin v hišah ob pragu in osem tisoč tristo pod podpisanimi strehami. Če bi se sto šestdeset streh umaknilo, bi rezerva zadoščala natančno. Če bi se jih več, bi Razsodnik odprl samo toliko, kolikor bi držale strehe, stara cestnina pa bi ostala odprta vsakomur, ki bi jo izbral.

**Hale**  
Ali vrata to zmorejo? Nastanitev nikoli ni bila vse.

**Razsodnik**  
Odprta tako široko kot ulica med zoro in mrakom spustijo deset tisoč ljudi. Vaš največji dan jih ima devet tisoč petsto. Štiristo zim sem vrata držal ozka, vendar nisem pozabil njihove širine. Število za vsak dan se odpre samo, če prejšnji dan ni prikril nobene kršitve zaveze. Če je katera prikrita, ta dan počaka, dokler zbor ne pove zakaj. Zadnji trije dnevi imajo prostora za šest tisoč ljudi več, kot ste jih vpisali, zato je mogoče kratek zastoj nadomestiti. Dolgega ni mogoče in to ve vsak na tem mostu. Hiše ob pragu ležijo v mojem vidnem polju. Sinoči sem jih preštel: postelje za sedemsto družin, niti ene več, in štejem jih skupaj s strehami.
Vsi na mostu so vedeli, kje lahko urnik spodleti in kje ne more.
Nekatere družine so vseeno plačale staro cestnino. Vdovec z dokov je šel prvi. Imele so svoje razloge in vrata so držala tudi zanje.

Hale je svoje palice položil na voz in vzel tablico ter košček krede. Rekel je, da bo prečkal zadnji, in nihče ga ni prosil za to. Stal je na začetku vrste in ljudi naglas štel skozi, po eno številko za vsakega.

Na drugi strani je Tam sedela na stebru vrat poleg ženske v modrem plašču in slabo žvižgala skozi travno bilko. Illuminara je stala na robu svetlobe, ki je bila za širino dlani širša kot včeraj, in poslušala štetje, ki se je nadaljevalo za njo v temi.

translation_sl.critic_line: Illuminara najprej spozna, da je Razsodnikova kruta cestnina dokazni sistem, zgrajen potem, ko se je resnična dobrodošlica končala v ognju, nato pa mu pomaga nepreverjeno žalost nadomestiti s prostovoljno gostiteljsko zavezo, dolinskim zborom, individualnim odpoklicem v varno hišo, ki bo preživela, in opaznim ravnanjem; Tam, Brannock, Greer, Hale, gostitelji in gostje ohranijo pomembne izbire, triinštirideset ljudi prečka celih, prva kršitev je popravljena brez kolektivnega kaznovanja, vrata in podpisane strehe lahko v devetih dneh sprejmejo vseh štirideset tisoč, prejšnji popotniki pa si lahko svobodno povrnejo tako ljubezen kot bolečino, ne da bi izbrisali zgodovino doline ali preostalo tveganje dolge prikrite kršitve.
